rashi:a1.1: A provisional guilt offering shall be burned: if he slaughtered it, and before the sprinkling of its blood it became known to him that he had not sinned, so that now it is a non-sacred animal slaughtered in the [Temple] courtyard. But if it did not become known to him, it is eaten like other guilt offerings, for the Merciful One called it a guilt offering in the portion of Vayikra, to atone for the uncertainty and to shield him from suffering until it becomes known to him that he certainly sinned and he brings a sin offering, as we say in Keritot, in the last chapter (26b).
rashi:a1.2: A sin offering of the bird, etc.: for example, a woman who miscarried, and it is uncertain whether it was a fetus or not a fetus. Since the sin offering [of a woman after childbirth] is [from] the bird, as it is written: “And a young pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering” [Leviticus 12:6], she brings it on account of the uncertainty: since it is not burned on the altar, we are not concerned if blood is sprinkled on account of an uncertainty. And it is not eaten, for perhaps it was not a fetus, and then this bird is non-sacred and is an unslaughtered carcass, as non-sacred birds are not eaten through pinching. And it shall be burned, since it is like other disqualified sacrificial items. And in Tractate Nazir (29a) we derive properly that a sin offering of the bird comes on account of an uncertainty.
rashi:a1.3: One should cast it into the drain: a channel of water passes through the [Temple] courtyard and goes out to the Kidron stream. And since [a young bird] is soft skin, it decomposes and does not hold together in the flow of the water.
rashi:a2.1: All items that are burned shall not be buried: lest a person come and find them and eat them.
rashi:a2.2: And items that are buried shall not be burned: the Gemara explains the reason.
rashi:a3.1: Gemara. A full sit: the full spread of the thumb from the finger, as far as one can spread them. [Rashi measures from the thumb; the Davidson English gives the distance between the index and middle fingers.]
rashi:a3.2: Wool of a firstborn: benefit from it is forbidden, for it is a sacrificial item.
rashi:a3.3: Shall be ignited: with wool it speaks of a garment and with hair it speaks of a sack, as is the usual way of things.
rashi:a3.4: The hair of a ritually pure nazirite shall be burned, for burning is written with regard to it, as it is written: “And put it on the fire,” etc. [Numbers 6:18]. With regard to the hair of a ritually impure nazirite, burning is not written.
rashi:a5.1: Here, in a sack: that which it teaches, “shall be ignited,” is where one wove hair of a nazirite and of a firstborn donkey into a sack, for if you were to say it is buried, a person would come and derive benefit from it, since it does not decay until after a long time. And our mishna is about the hair itself, which was not woven. And both this and that are about a pure or an impure [nazirite].
rashi:a6.1: And Rabbi Elazar says, etc.: and both this and that are about a sack. And as for the firstborn donkey, the Gemara resolves it below and establishes it in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:a7.1: Let it be nullified by the majority: for it teaches “the hair of a nazirite and a firstborn donkey in a sack,” implying a little of it in a large garment of permitted material. And if you ask about what we say in Tractate Nidda (61b), that a garment in which a thread of diverse kinds was lost may not be sold to a gentile: why is it forbidden to sell it? Let that thread be nullified by the majority, just as we say here! That is no refutation, for with regard to diverse kinds one does not say “let it be nullified by the majority,” since the Torah forbade diverse kinds essentially only through a mixture, and we translate kilayim [in Aramaic] as “mixtures,” so nullification does not apply to them.
rashi:a7.2: With a bird: that he made from the forbidden material the shape of a bird in the sack, which is significant, as it beautifies the whole sack, and it is not nullified.
rashi:a8.1: In accordance with whom is this: for now it enters our mind that he resolves it this way: in accordance with whom is this ruling, which goes toward stringency? It is Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:a8.2: He said to him: It is difficult for us, “let him remove them”: for a remedy is possible, and you establish it in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda? Where there is a remedy, did Rabbi Yehuda say [one may burn]? He said to him: This is what I am saying: if it is possible to remove them, fine. And as for what posed a difficulty for you, firstborn donkey against firstborn donkey, that here it teaches “shall be burned” and in our mishna “shall be buried”: do not resolve it with the nazirite (here an impure one, there a pure one); rather, establish all of it in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, and it is properly resolved.
tosafot:a9.1: If it is possible to remove them, fine: this does not refer at all to the difficulty “let them be nullified by the majority,” but to the first difficulty, that there it teaches “shall be ignited” and in our mishna “shall be buried”; and the wording is not exact.
rashi:a13.1: What is the reason that items that are buried shall not be burned? Because the ash of items that are buried is forbidden, and people would come to permit it.
tosafot:a13.1: And items that are burned are permitted: (consecrated property is difficult). It is fine if we read “items that are burned, their ash is permitted” [without mention of consecrated property], and so we read in some books. However, it can be reconciled: they took the ash of consecrated property here to strengthen the point, [namely the ash] of our mishna’s [sacrificial animals] slaughtered beyond their time, whose ash is permitted; and because just below the Gemara raises an objection from them, saying “And items of consecrated property that are burned, is their ash permitted?”, the tanna took it up here.
rashi:a14.1: The blood of a menstruating woman and the flesh of a corpse: even though we hold, in Tractate Nidda (54b), that they render impure whether moist or dry, where they have become mere ash they are pure, if there is not a full ladle of corpse dust there; and [the questioner takes it that] benefit from them is permitted. And the flesh of a corpse is among the items that are buried, yet its ash is permitted.
rashi:a15.1: Whose blood was squeezed: whose mitzva has been performed.
rashi:a15.2: Its crop and its feathers: they are among the items that are buried, as we say in the first chapter of Yoma (21a): the crop and the feathers, and the ashes removed from the inner altar and from the Candelabrum, are swallowed up in their place.
rashi:a15.3: And are permitted: even initially, if one dug and took them.
rashi:a16.1: All items that are burned: such as leavened bread, teruma, orla and diverse kinds of the vineyard; their ash is permitted for laundering clothes.
rashi:a16.2: Is prohibited forever; and he did not combine, etc.: the one raising this difficulty goes on to explain the baraita, so that it should not itself pose a difficulty for him: since the ash of ashera wood and the ash of consecrated property are both forbidden, why does it separate them from each other, and not teach “except for ashera wood and ash of consecrated property” without teaching “is prohibited forever”? And he explains: because they are not alike, for an ashera can be nullified by a gentile, as we hold in Tractate Avoda Zara: from where is it derived that a gentile can disqualify his god? For it is written “the carved images of their gods” and it is written “and take it for yourself” [Deuteronomy 7:25], in the chapter Rabbi Yishmael (Avoda Zara 52a), in the Gemara on “An idol belonging to a gentile is forbidden,” etc.
rashi:a18.1: This is the reading: “there is no person who misused.” For if a person had kindled it, the one who lit it would have misused it, and the ash would go out to non-sacred status. And as for those items that require burning, even without any misuse their ash goes out to non-sacred status, since their sanctity is weakened, as they have been disqualified. And that which it teaches, “ash of consecrated property is forbidden,” is where there is no misuse and there is no person who misused, and it speaks of consecrated wood.
rashi:a19.1: When this was taught: that the ash of consecrated property is forbidden, it speaks of the full handful of the ashes that the priest removes every day in the morning and places beside the altar, as it says in the second chapter of Yoma (24a): it is stated here “and he shall take up” and it is stated there “and he shall take up”; just as there it is with his handful, so too here it is with his handful.
rashi:a20.1: “And he shall put them” beside the altar; “and he shall put them,” all of it: and since it requires storing away, benefit from it is forbidden.
gershom:a1.1: Rav Tavi said to him: And with a sack, why should the sack be ignited? Let this hair be nullified by the majority in the sack. [Rabbeinu Gershom puts this challenge in the mouth of Tavi, whom he calls Rav Tavi; the Davidson English gives it to Rav Naḥman.]
gershom:a2.1: Rav Pappa said: With a bird: for example, one wove from that nazirite hair, in the sack, the image of a bird, which is significant work; therefore it is not nullified, and it shall be ignited.
gershom:a3.1: And still, why should it be ignited? Let him pull that hair out of the sack and bury it, and the sack need not be burned.
gershom:a4.1: In accordance with whom is this, that it shall be burned? It is Rabbi Yehuda, who said in our mishna: “If he wished to impose a stringency,” etc. He said to him: It is difficult for us, “let him remove them,” for I am seeking to give it a remedy so that it is not burned at all, and you establish it in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, that it shall be burned!
gershom:a5.1: He said to him: This is what I am saying: if it is possible to remove them, fine, so that it is not burned; and if it is not possible to remove them, [it shall be ignited]: establish this mishna, which teaches “shall be ignited,” in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who said: “If he wished to impose a stringency,” etc.
gershom:a6.1: One may say: when Rabbi Yehuda said “if he wished to impose a stringency,” that is when the items are by themselves; but a buried item in a mixture, such as this sack, did you hear him say that it is burned? [The answer:] the tanna teaches that if he did not wish to pull it out and bury it, but rather to burn it all together, he may, in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
gershom:a7.1: That whose way is to be burned, such as foods, shall be burned; and that whose way is to be buried, such as liquids, which cannot be burned, shall be buried.
gershom:a8.1: One may light the lamp with the oil and the baked bread (the oven): that is, the priest derives benefit from impure teruma for kindling. And should we not be concerned that if he keeps the teruma for kindling, it may lead him to a stumbling block, lest he eat it? [This refers to the clause of the mishna on 33b permitting one to ignite a fire with bread and oil of impure teruma.]
gershom:a9.1: Bread: he throws it among the wood, and it is evident that it is no longer fit for eating; and oil, in a repulsive vessel. [Reading with the bracketed corrections in the printed text.]
gershom:a10.1: A provisional guilt offering that was disqualified shall be burned, in accordance with the law of other sacrificial items, since it is eaten by the priests like a definite guilt offering.
gershom:a11.1: Rabbi Yehuda says: It shall be buried: because it is taught in a baraita in the Gemara together with non-sacred animals slaughtered in the [Temple] courtyard, and we already said in the mishna above that non-sacred animals slaughtered in the courtyard shall be buried.
gershom:a12.1: A sin offering of the bird that comes due to an uncertainty: for example, a woman after childbirth, uncertain whether [she bore] a male or a female, or uncertain whether she miscarried a fetus or miscarried a wind, or a woman uncertain whether she is a zava: she brings an offering, and it is not eaten.
gershom:a13.1: Shall be burned: since she is obligated to bring it, its law is like that of other disqualified sacrificial items, which are burned. Rabbi Yehuda says: One should cast it into the water channel that runs down to the Kidron stream, and this is its burial. He holds that since it is not eaten, it is not burned but buried, like other items that are buried, whose prohibition is only in eating.
gershom:a14.1: The Sages taught: a provisional guilt offering and a sin offering of the bird that comes due to an uncertainty. Since it teaches them together with non-sacred animals slaughtered in the [Temple] courtyard, Rabbi Yehuda holds that they shall be buried. And it speaks of a guilt offering that became disqualified, for if it did not become disqualified it is eaten, as it is taught in Tractate Keritot: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, says: A provisional guilt offering is eaten; a sin offering of the bird that comes due to an uncertainty is not eaten. What is the reason? A provisional guilt offering has only one uncertainty: perhaps it is sacred, perhaps non-sacred, for perhaps he ate forbidden fat, perhaps it was permitted fat; so it has only the uncertainty of a non-sacred animal slaughtered in the courtyard, and therefore it is eaten. And further, because we say that a person may volunteer and bring a provisional guilt offering every day, for if it does not come for this sin, it comes for another sin.
gershom:a15.1: But a sin offering of the bird has two uncertainties of prohibition: perhaps it is a non-sacred bird in the courtyard, and perhaps it carries the prohibition of an unslaughtered carcass, since it was pinched; for if it is non-sacred, it is forbidden as a carcass. Therefore it is not eaten.
gershom:a16.1: Items that are buried: those whose law is to be buried, if one burned them, their ash is forbidden. Therefore it is forbidden to change, for if he were to burn them, people would derive benefit from their ash, as we hold that the ash of items that are burned is permitted.
gershom:a17.1: The blood of a menstruating woman and the flesh of a corpse, whose way is to be buried: if they were not buried and had already crumbled by themselves and become ash, they are permitted. [What, is it not that they are pure and] their ash is permitted for benefit?
gershom:a18.1: A burnt offering of the bird whose blood was squeezed onto the wall of the altar: its crop and its feathers, which are not burned on the altar, have gone out from misuse, for they already have a time of permission: they have no mitzva of burning on the altar, and their mitzva has already been performed, as no mitzva remains in them; therefore they have gone out from misuse. But one is liable for misuse of its flesh itself until it goes out to the place of the ashes, since its mitzva is not performed until it is burned, and it has no time of permission for the priests, as it is entirely burned. And these, the crop and the feathers, are among the items that are buried, as we learned: the crop and the feathers are swallowed into the ground in their place by a miracle. And it teaches that they have gone out from misuse: what, is it not that they have gone out from misuse and are permitted?
gershom:a19.1: No: they have gone out [from misuse] and are forbidden. And the reason he does not combine them, saying “except for ashera wood and ash of consecrated property,” but goes back and says “and ash of consecrated property is prohibited forever,” is because an ashera can be nullified by a gentile: if a gentile nullifies it, it is permitted.
gershom:a20.1: With what are we dealing here, that ash of consecrated property is prohibited forever? For example, where a fire fell by itself onto consecrated property, so there was no person who misused it whose misuse would take the ash out to non-sacred status. For this is the law of misuse: if it is an item whose mitzva is burning, once he burned it, its mitzva has been performed, there is no misuse in it, and its ash is permitted. And if it is an item whose mitzva is not burning, once he burned it, since he misused it, it went out to non-sacred status and its ash is permitted. But when a fire fell by itself, since no person misused it, it did not go out to non-sacred status; therefore that ash of consecrated property is prohibited forever. And this is the reason that one who misuses is liable to bring an offering for misuse: since he misused it, he took it out to non-sacred status, and for that reason he brings an offering for misuse, for he took consecrated property out to non-sacred status.
gershom:a21.1: Rav Shemaya said: When that was taught, that ash of consecrated property is prohibited forever, it was with regard to the removal of the ashes. Another version: that is, ash that requires storing away.
gershom:a22.1: As it is taught: “And he shall put them beside the altar.” It could have said “and he shall put” beside the altar; rather, one “and he shall put them” is needed for “he shall put all of it,” and the other “and he shall put them,” which comes from the vav, is needed for “he shall put them gently,” so that he does not scatter them. Concluded.
